newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Voting in Bosnia begins, quickly hits trouble.
newsitem.headline: Voting in Bosnia begins, quickly hits trouble.

text.p: Voting began on Saturday in Bosnian elections aimed at healing the wounds of war but quickly ran into trouble when Serbs were reported to be stopping some refugees trying to vote.
Witnesses said most of the 4,600 polling stations across the country appeared to open on time at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT), though early voting was light.

Serb refugees arrived in Bosnia through the night, brought by train from Belgrade to vote in the Bosnian Serb Republic. They were shepherded through the dark onto buses to be taken to polling stations.

But the voting, organised by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) and policed by 60,000 NATO-led peace troops, quickly ran into trouble, with Serbs reported to have blocked one of 19 designated routes and a crossing point.
Chief OSCE organiser Jeff Fischer said Serb police had refused to open a route to the Prijedor area in north-west Bosnia, a Serb stronghold, adding negotiations were going on.
A spokesman for the IFOR peace force said Serb police were also preventing refugee voters from coming over a bridge from Croatia to the northeastern Serb-controlled town of Brcko.

In another incident, Fischer said the main nationalist Croat party HDZ had pulled out all its poll workers from the Moslem-controlled town of Bugojno after a grenade attack on the home of the local electoral committee chairman, a Croat.
Fischer said voting was proceeding normally in the town despite the incident.

At one polling station in central Sarajevo, seven elderly people were waiting outside as its doors swung open. The first couple to vote said they were refugees from Pale -- the Bosnian Serb stronghold a short drive from Saraejevo.

Some 2.9 million Moslems, Croats and Serbs will elect a national presidency and parliament, a president and separate parliament for the Serb Republic, and a parliament and cantonal administrations in the Moslem-Croat Federation.

At a bus depot in Sarajevo, four refugees sat anxiously waiting to be driven back to their old home districts to vote, the first time they have returned since they were driven out by the ethnic cleansing which marked the 3-1/2 war.
The biggest short-term fear of the international community was of violence between ethnic rivals meeting one another on Saturday in places they once fought over.

The United States has led a chorus of senior Western officials in publicly proclaiming the country has no choice but to go through with the elections, however flawed, if it is ever to recover from the conflict.
